one_liner: GNU C library; its CPU-dispatched string routines, malloc, qsort, regexec and strtod beat zig-bundled static musl in most micro-benchmarks.
what_it_does: glibc is the system C library of most Linux distributions, so a C++ program built for *-linux-gnu already uses it for str*/mem*, malloc, qsort, regex, strtod and stdio. It is not a library you add: the choice it represents is the libc target (glibc versus musl, as used by Alpine images, zig cc and static Rust/Go builds). The API is the same ISO C/POSIX surface as musl, so moving code between them is a target and link change rather than a code change.
how_it_is_fast: On x86-64 the string and memory functions are hand-written assembly variants (SSE2, AVX2, EVEX/AVX-512) picked once at load time through IFUNC from CPU feature bits: in 2.35, strstr resolves to __strstr_sse2_unaligned, which scans 64 bytes per loop iteration for the needle's first two bytes, and memmove/memcpy switch to rep movsb above 2112 bytes on FSRM CPUs (dl-cacheinfo.h). malloc puts a per-thread cache (tcache: 64 size bins, 7 chunks each) in front of the ptmalloc2 arenas; qsort is a merge sort with a temporary buffer (alloca under 1 KB, malloc above, quicksort fallback); regexec runs a DFA-state matcher; strtod converts exactly with multi-precision (mpn) arithmetic. The musl side loses on plain C loops by comparison: word-at-a-time stpcpy for strcpy, smoothsort for qsort, a two-way matcher for strstr.
when_to_use: You ship dynamically linked binaries for mainstream Linux distributions: glibc is already the libc and costs nothing to adopt.

Deciding between a glibc and a musl target for code heavy in strcpy/strncpy/strncmp, regexec, strtod, qsort or small malloc/free: glibc measured 2.8x (qsort of 4096 ints) to 37x (strncmp) faster in this run, 11x on 32-byte malloc/free.
Long string copies and compares on x86-64, where the per-CPU AVX2/EVEX variants pay off (strcpy of 2047 bytes: 22 ns vs 129 ns).
Parsing-heavy code (strtod 4.3x, regexec 5.9x, getline 3.5x faster than the musl build) where you cannot swap in a specialised parser.
when_not_to_use: Fully static, portable binaries: static glibc carries LGPL obligations and breaks NSS and iconv module loading; musl is the usual static choice.

Large memcpy on AMD Zen 3/Zen 4 with a glibc that predates the BZ 30994 fix (2.35 as on Ubuntu 22.04): the 16 KB copy ran 26x slower (4043 vs 154 ns) because rep movsb hits page aliasing; upgrade, or raise glibc.cpu.x86_rep_movsb_threshold through GLIBC_TUNABLES.

Workloads dominated by strtok/strtok_r (2.7x and 3.0x slower than the musl build), atoi (2.3x slower), bsearch (1.5x slower) or strrchr over long strings with many matches (2.25x slower on glibc 2.35).
Medium (4 KB) allocation churn: ptmalloc2 took 828 ns per malloc/free against 81 ns for jemalloc linked into the musl build; link jemalloc or mimalloc instead of relying on the default allocator.
Footprint-constrained containers or embedded images where musl's much smaller runtime matters more than these speedups.

integration.dependencies: Linux kernel 3.2 or later (glibc 2.35 README); otherwise none, it is the system libc
integration.min_toolchain: any C/C++ toolchain targeting *-linux-gnu (the benchmark used zig cc -target x86_64-linux-gnu); building glibc itself not covered here
integration.platforms: Linux on x86-64, aarch64, arm, ppc, riscv, s390 and others (README configuration list), plus GNU/Hurd; SIMD string variants are per architecture and chosen at load time by IFUNC on x86-64
integration.thread_safety: malloc is thread-safe with per-thread tcache and arenas; strtok keeps hidden static state (use strtok_r); other functions follow POSIX thread-safety rules
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: same ISO C/POSIX API as musl, so switching is a target/link change, but static linking, locale/NSS behaviour and GNU extensions differ

gotchas: The baseline is not pure musl: zig 0.15.2 replaces musl's memcpy, memmove, strlen, strcmp and strncmp with Zig code (lib/c/string.zig, compiler_rt memcpy.zig). The 37x strncmp win is against Zig's byte-at-a-time loop, the memcpy loss is against Zig's compiler_rt memcpy, and musl's strrchr win (musl calls memrchr(s, c, strlen(s)+1)) rides on Zig's SIMD strlen (std.mem.indexOfSentinel).

memcpy speed depends on the glibc version and the CPU: 2.35 uses rep movsb from 2112 bytes up to the L2 size on AMD (dl-cacheinfo.h). On Zen 3/4 that hits BZ 30994 page aliasing when (dst-src) mod 4096 is small, as with two adjacent 16 KB heap blocks. The fix 'x86: Fix Zen3/Zen4 ERMS selection' landed on the 2.39 branch (search snippets only; sourceware.org not opened).

glibc qsort through 2.38 can corrupt memory when the comparator is non-transitive (for example a - b on ints) and its temporary-buffer malloc fails, which sends it to the _quicksort fallback (Qualys advisory 2024-01-30; glibc treats the comparator as the bug). qsort also mallocs a temporary buffer of 1 KB or more, so it allocates on every large call.

Harness flaws behind several rows: strlen, strcmp and memcmp are hoisted no-ops (about 0.1 ns). vprintf_mix never calls vprintf; it calls vsnprintf with another format. file_io_rw times tmpfile() disk I/O. The strstr_search averages are implausible for the source: 10 of 16 needles scan the about 16 KB haystack that strcpy's NUL leaves, so glibc's 36.28 ns average implies about 282 bytes/ns, beyond what the SSE2 loop in strstr-sse2-unaligned.S (eight 16-byte loads per 64 bytes) can deliver. The cause was not found and was not reproduced (derived from benchmark.c and page data).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: glibc is the libc you already link, so it is the baseline those siblings beat. Reach for StringZilla or sse4-strstr when substring search dominates: glibc 2.35's x86-64 strstr only chooses between two SSE2 versions. Reach for the Boost.Algorithm Boyer-Moore searchers when one long pattern is searched in many haystacks.
verified_claims_summary: fereidani/musl-vs-glibc built one C benchmark with zig 0.15.2 (clang 20.1.2, -O3 -march=native -flto=full) against the host's dynamic glibc (Ubuntu 22.04 kernel string, so probably 2.35) and against zig's static musl, then ran each binary once (250 ms calibrated target per row) on an AMD Ryzen 7 PRO 5850U. glibc was fastest in 17 of 32 rows (strncmp 37x, strcpy 5.9x, strncpy 5.4x, regexec 5.9x, strtod 4.3x, qsort 2.8x, 32-byte malloc/free 11.4x, derived from page data) and lost memcpy (26x), strrchr, strtok, strtok_r, atoi, bsearch and sprintf_float.
status_note: glibc is actively developed upstream at sourceware.org; the bminor GitHub mirror used as repo_url was archived on 2026-02-15 and is read-only, and the library is LGPL-2.1-or-later and used as the system shared library rather than vendored. The evidence is one unrepeated hobby run whose musl column partly measures Zig's own memcpy/strlen/strcmp/strncmp, whose memcpy row reflects a Zen 3 glibc bug fixed in later versions, and whose strstr row is implausibly fast for the code it times.
